parole.testo: Borrowed from Neapolitan, from Vulgar Latin *plattus, from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús, “broad, flat”), from Proto-Indo-European *pléth₂us, from *pleth₂- (“flat”). Doublet of piatto (“flat”).

Possibly, through Neapolitan, from Latin phalanga (“pole for carrying things”, by extension “pole for sustaining grapevine”), from Ancient Greek φᾰ́λᾰγξ (phắlănx, “line, rank”), Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵ- (“beam, plank”). Compare falanga and falange.

parole.significato: fumarole (opening in the ground that emits gases)
parole.testo: From Neapolitan fumarola, from Late Latin fūmāriolum, diminutive of fūmārium (“chimney”), from Latin fumus (“smoke”), 16th c. Compare Sicilian fumalora.

Borrowed from Neapolitan, the equivalent of Italian immondizia and immondezza, from Latin immunditia (“dirt, untidiness”), from immundus (“dirty”), from im- (“without, not”) + mundus (“clean, elegant”). Doublet of immondizia and immondezza. Compare Sicilian munnizza.
From Neapolitan pernacchio, from earlier vernacchio, from Latin vernāculus (“of or pertaining to a slave”). Doublet of vernacolo.
From the present participle of pezzire, from (Old) Neapolitan pezzire, from Vulgar Latin *petīre, from Latin petere.

parole.significato: a pigeon; more accurately the rock pigeon, feral pigeon or domestic pigeon
parole.testo: Borrowed from Neapolitan piccione, from Latin pīpiōnem. Doublet of pippione.

parole.significato: droveway, sheep track, commonly found in Southern Italy
parole.testo: Borrowed from Neapolitan, from Latin tractōrius (“of or relating to drawing and hoisting”), from trahō, trahere (“to draw, hoist”), whence Italian trarre.
Borrowed from Neapolitan vongola, from Latin conchula, from concha. Displaced Old Italian gongola.
